title: Cellular respiration
summary: How does a cell transfer the energy in food to ATP?
cards.0.h: The structure and cycle of ATP
cards.0.p: ATP is made of adenine, ribose and three phosphates. When the last phosphate is split off by hydrolysis, energy is released and ATP becomes ADP. When a phosphate is added back to ADP, ATP forms again.
cards.0.svg#9: breakdown releases energy · rebuilding needs energy
cards.0.key: Active transport and synthesis reactions also run on ATP. The energy comes from the whole hydrolysis reaction, not just from breaking the bond.
cards.0.once.soru: When a muscle contracts, which molecule directly supplies the energy it uses?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: The energy of glucose is first transferred to ATP. The muscle then spends this ATP.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Glucose is not used directly. Its energy is first transferred to ATP.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: O₂ does not supply energy. In respiration it acts as the electron acceptor.
cards.1.p: Adding a phosphate to ADP is called phosphorylation. In substrate-level phosphorylation, the phosphate comes from an organic molecule. Oxidative phosphorylation uses the energy of the electron transport chain (ETC), and photophosphorylation uses the energy of light.
cards.1.svg#18: most ATP in respiration comes from the oxidative route
cards.1.key: Substrate-level phosphorylation happens in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. ATP synthase works in oxidative phosphorylation and photophosphorylation, but not in substrate-level phosphorylation.
cards.1.once.soru: What is it called when a chloroplast makes ATP with light energy?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: Photophosphorylation uses light energy and happens in the chloroplast during photosynthesis.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Oxidative phosphorylation happens in the mitochondrion, using the energy of the ETC.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: Substrate-level phosphorylation is the transfer of a phosphate from an organic molecule to ADP.
cards.2.p: In aerobic respiration, glucose is broken down completely: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and the ETC in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
cards.2.svg#12: O₂ is used only in the last stage (ETC)
cards.2.svg#13: part of the energy goes to ATP, the rest becomes heat
cards.2.key: Pyruvate oxidation also takes place in the matrix. NAD⁺ and FAD carry electrons and hydrogens to the ETC as NADH and FADH₂. In prokaryotes, the stages run in the cytoplasm and the ETC runs in the cell membrane.
cards.3.p: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and does not need O₂. Six-carbon glucose is split into two three-carbon pyruvates. Along the way, 2 ATP are spent and 4 ATP are made. So there is a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
cards.3.svg#6: in the cytoplasm · no O₂ needed · in nearly all living things
cards.3.key: Because glycolysis does not need O₂, it occurs in nearly every living thing. The NADH made in glycolysis goes to the ETC if O₂ is present. Otherwise it is used up in fermentation.
cards.4.p: If O₂ is present, pyruvate moves into the mitochondrial matrix. One CO₂ is removed from each pyruvate and one NADH forms. The remaining two-carbon group becomes acetyl-CoA.
cards.4.key: This step happens twice for each glucose. The first CO₂ of respiration is released in this step, not in glycolysis.
cards.5.p: The Krebs cycle turns in the matrix. Acetyl-CoA joins with oxaloacetate. One turn makes 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 ATP. For one glucose, the cycle turns twice.
cards.5.svg#18: in the matrix · oxaloacetate (4C) is regenerated
cards.5.key: Two-carbon acetyl-CoA joins four-carbon oxaloacetate to form six-carbon citrate, and the oxaloacetate is regenerated. The ATP in the Krebs cycle is made by substrate-level phosphorylation.
cards.5.once.soru: How many turns does the Krebs cycle make for one glucose?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Glucose gives two pyruvates, and those give two acetyl-CoA.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: One glucose gives two acetyl-CoA, and each one turns the cycle once.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Glucose has 6 carbons, but the cycle takes in acetyl groups two carbons at a time.
cards.6.p: In the inner mitochondrial membrane, NADH and FADH₂ hand their electrons to a chain. The energy of these electrons pumps H⁺ ions. As the H⁺ ions flow back through ATP synthase, ATP is made. The final electron acceptor is O₂.
cards.6.key: H⁺ ions build up in the intermembrane space and create a proton gradient. In respiration, water forms in the ETC. CO₂ is released in pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle.
cards.6.once.soru: What does the oxygen we breathe do in the cell?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: At the end of the ETC, O₂ takes the electrons and H⁺ ions and forms water.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Blood carries glucose. O₂ works in the ETC.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The CO₂ we breathe out comes from the carbons of glucose. O₂ becomes water.
cards.7.p: Most ATP is made in the ETC. One NADH gives about 2.5 ATP and one FADH₂ about 1.5 ATP. This makes a total of about 30-32 ATP. Older textbooks give this number as 36-38.
cards.7.key: Only 4 ATP come directly from glucose. The older count takes one NADH as 3 ATP and one FADH₂ as 2 ATP. The gap between 30 and 32 depends on how the NADH from glycolysis is carried into the mitochondrion.
cards.7.etk.soru: Change the ATP value used for one NADH and one FADH<sub>2</sub>. One glucose gives 10 NADH, 2 FADH<sub>2</sub> and 4 ATP directly.
cards.7.etk.yorum.0.1: With current values you get at most 32 ATP. Depending on how the NADH from glycolysis enters the mitochondrion, the result is about 30-32 ATP.
cards.7.etk.yorum.1.1: Current and older values are mixed here.
cards.7.etk.yorum.2.1: This is the older textbook count, which gives 36-38 ATP.
cards.7.once.soru: Each glucose makes 10 NADH. If one NADH gives about 2.5 ATP, how much ATP comes from the NADH?
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: Each NADH gives more than one ATP.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: That is the ATP from just one NADH.
cards.8.p: Without O₂, NAD⁺ runs out and glycolysis stops. In fermentation, pyruvate is reduced by NADH, which regenerates NAD⁺. This keeps glycolysis going. But ATP comes only from glycolysis, so the yield is a net 2 ATP.
cards.8.svg#8: in the cytoplasm · no ETC · no O₂
cards.8.key: Fermentation takes place in the cytoplasm. Some books also call fermentation "anaerobic respiration". However, the anaerobic respiration of some bacteria does use an ETC.
cards.9.p: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast turns pyruvate into ethyl alcohol and CO₂. This CO₂ is what makes dough rise. Lactic acid fermentation is carried out by yogurt bacteria and tired muscle cells, and it produces lactic acid.
cards.9.key: The alcohol in dough evaporates in the oven. Lactic acid fermentation releases no CO₂. The muscle soreness you feel the next day comes from small injuries in the muscle, not from lactic acid.
cards.10.p: Both processes start with glycolysis, and they differ after pyruvate. In aerobic respiration, glucose is broken down all the way to CO₂ and water. The products of fermentation still carry energy, so its yield is low.
cards.10.svg#20: both start with glycolysis, the difference comes after pyruvate
cards.10.key: Some organisms, such as yeast, can do both depending on conditions. Because ethyl alcohol still carries energy, it is also used as a fuel.
cards.10.etk.soru: Does each feature belong to aerobic respiration, to fermentation, or to both?
cards.10.etk.ogeler.4.0: Product is alcohol or lactic acid
cards.10.etk.ogeler.7.2: All of fermentation happens in the cytoplasm, and mitochondria are not used.
cards.10.etk.ogeler.8.2: Yeast can do both depending on conditions. With O<sub>2</sub> it respires aerobically, and without it, it ferments.
cards.11.h: Fats and proteins are burned too
cards.11.p: Cells also use fats and proteins for energy. Glycerol joins glycolysis, and fatty acids enter the Krebs cycle as acetyl-CoA. Amino acids first lose their nitrogen group, and the rest enters the Krebs pathway.
cards.11.key: The nitrogen group becomes ammonia first and then urea. The rest becomes pyruvate, acetyl-CoA or an intermediate of the Krebs cycle.
cards.11.once.soru: Which gives the most energy per gram?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: Fat gives about 9 kcal per gram. Carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: Carbohydrate gives about 4 kcal per gram. That is less than half of what fat gives.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Protein gives about 4 kcal per gram. That is less than half of what fat gives.
cards.12.p: Photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose. Respiration breaks this glucose down and transfers its energy to ATP. The products of one are the inputs of the other. Plants respire day and night.
cards.12.svg#9: photosynthesis: light energy → chemical energy of glucose
cards.12.svg#10: respiration: chemical energy of glucose → ATP
cards.12.key: The equation of photosynthesis is 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O, and photosynthesis happens only in light. At the light compensation point, photosynthesis and respiration run at the same rate, so there is no net gas exchange.
cards.13.p:
• ATP gives energy by turning into ADP and phosphate. It is the energy currency of the cell.
• Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the matrix, and the ETC in the inner membrane.
• The final electron acceptor is O₂, and the total is about 30-32 ATP.
• Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ and gives a net 2 ATP.
• Photosynthesis and respiration produce each other's inputs.
quiz.0.q: Group each event by where it happens in the cell.
quiz.0.e: Glycolysis and fermentation happen in the cytoplasm. The Krebs cycle, including the formation of citrate from acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate, runs in the mitochondrial matrix. The ETC and ATP synthase work in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
quiz.1.q: A muscle cell breaks down 4 glucose by aerobic respiration and 6 glucose by lactic acid fermentation. If aerobic respiration gives 30 ATP per glucose, how much net ATP does the cell gain in total?
quiz.1.e: Aerobic respiration gives 4 × 30 = 120 ATP. Fermentation gives only the net 2 ATP of glycolysis per glucose: 6 × 2 = 12 ATP. The total is 132 ATP.
quiz.2.q: Put in order what happens to a glucose in aerobic respiration.
quiz.2.ogeler.0: Glucose splits into two pyruvates in the cytoplasm
quiz.2.ogeler.1: CO₂ is removed from pyruvate and acetyl-CoA forms
quiz.2.ogeler.2: Acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate and citrate forms
quiz.2.ogeler.3: NADH and FADH₂ from the Krebs cycle give electrons to the ETC
quiz.2.ogeler.4: H⁺ is pumped into the intermembrane space
quiz.2.ogeler.5: ATP is made as H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase
quiz.2.e: The order is glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle and the ETC. In the ETC, the energy of the electrons pumps H⁺. ATP is made as the H⁺ ions flow back through ATP synthase.
quiz.3.q: In a closed container with glucose, yeast first uses up the O₂ inside. What is observed after the O₂ runs out completely?
quiz.3.o.2: Water formation in the ETC speeds up.
quiz.3.o.3: CO₂ release continues and ethyl alcohol builds up.
quiz.3.e: When the O₂ runs out, yeast switches to alcoholic fermentation. CO₂ release continues and alcohol builds up. Because the ETC stops, water formation there stops too.
quiz.3.y.0: Without oxygen, yeast switches to fermentation. Alcoholic fermentation also releases CO₂.
quiz.3.y.1: Yeast does alcoholic fermentation, not lactic acid fermentation. Lactic acid fermentation is seen in muscle cells and yogurt bacteria.
quiz.3.y.2: When the O₂ runs out, the ETC has no final electron acceptor. Water formation stops and fermentation begins.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Break down glucose step by step, count the ATP and cut off the oxygen.
A:adimlar.0.metin: In aerobic respiration, glucose is broken down all the way to CO₂ and water. The stages are glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the matrix and the ETC in the inner membrane. Press play.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: In which stage is most ATP made?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Glycolysis gives only a few ATP. The real gain comes later.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The Krebs cycle gives only 2 ATP over two turns.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Using the energy of electrons taken from glucose, most of the ATP, about 26-28, is made in the ETC.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Play glycolysis, which splits glucose in two, and watch the ATP counter.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP. Why is the net gain 2 ATP?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: 2 ATP are spent at the start
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: 2 ATP are spent first to prepare glucose for the reaction. So 4 − 2 = 2 ATP remain.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: ATP does not leave with CO₂. No CO₂ is released in glycolysis either. The first CO₂ is released in pyruvate oxidation.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: NADH is the reduced form of NAD⁺ and is not made from ATP.
A:adimlar.2.metin: If O₂ is present, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion. First comes pyruvate oxidation, then the Krebs cycle turns twice. Step through the stages and watch the counters.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: All 6 carbons of glucose have become CO₂. Two were released in pyruvate oxidation and four in the Krebs cycle. A total of 10 NADH and 2 FADH₂ built up, and their energy will be turned into ATP in the ETC.
A:adimlar.3.metin: There is no O₂. Play the ETC.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: With no final electron acceptor, electrons pile up in the chain and the chain stops completely.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The Krebs cycle needs NAD⁺. When NAD⁺ runs low, the cycle does not speed up, it stops.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: With no O₂ to take the electrons, NADH cannot turn back into NAD⁺. When NAD⁺ runs out, the Krebs cycle and glycolysis stop too.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Play the yeast first, then switch to the muscle cell and play again.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: What is the difference between the two fermentations?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: In both, ATP comes only from glycolysis, and one glucose gives a net 2 ATP.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Yeast turns pyruvate into ethyl alcohol and CO₂, while the muscle cell turns it into lactic acid.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The purpose of both fermentations is to regenerate NAD⁺ and keep glycolysis going.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Fermentation gives a net 2 ATP per glucose, and its products still carry energy. Aerobic respiration gives about 30 ATP per glucose. How many glucose does fermentation need to give the same amount of ATP?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: Each glucose gives 2 ATP. For 30 ATP, divide 30 by 2.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: 15 glucose × 2 ATP = 30 ATP. So a fermenting cell burns about 15 times as much glucose for the same ATP.
A:adimlar.6.baslik: A plant by day and night
A:adimlar.6.metin: A plant cell does both photosynthesis and respiration. Compare its gas exchange by day and by night.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Why does a plant give off O₂ during the day?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Respiration goes on day and night in a living cell. It does not stop during the day.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: Respiration uses O₂ only at night
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Aerobic respiration uses O₂ all the time, because O₂ is the final electron acceptor of the ETC.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: By day both processes run together. But photosynthesis makes more O₂ than respiration uses.
A:kapanis.0: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, needs no O₂ and gives a net 2 ATP.
A:kapanis.1: The carbons of glucose are released as CO₂ in pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle.
A:kapanis.2: Most ATP is made in the ETC, and the final electron acceptor is O₂. The total is about 30-32 ATP.
A:kapanis.3: Without O₂, fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ but gives only 2 ATP.
A:kapanis.4: A plant respires day and night. In light, photosynthesis is faster than respiration.
